points: Japan launched a surprise military attack on Pearl Harbor.
The attack took place on December 7, 1941.
The attack targeted the US Pacific Fleet at its naval base on Oahu, Hawaii.
The United States was neutral in World War II when the attack occurred.
The Pearl Harbor air raid was launched from aircraft carriers.
The attack prompted the United States to declare war on Japan the next day.
Japanese military leaders called the attack the Hawaii Operation.
Japanese military leaders also called the attack Operation AI.
During planning, the attack was called Operation Z.
The attack followed months of US–Japanese negotiations over the future of the Pacific.
Japan demanded that the United States end its sanctions against Japan.
Japan demanded that the United States stop aiding China in the Second Sino-Japanese War.
Japan demanded US acceptance of Japanese access to the resources of the Dutch East Indies.
Japan dispatched its attack force on November 26, 1941, just before receiving the Hull note.
The Hull note called for Japan to withdraw from China.
The Hull note called for Japan to withdraw from French Indochina.
Isoroku Yamamoto commanded Japan's Combined Fleet.
Yamamoto planned the attack as a preemptive strike to stop the US Pacific Fleet from interfering with Japan's military plans in Southeast Asia.
The Pacific Fleet had been based at Pearl Harbor since 1940.
Yamamoto hoped the strike would let Japan make rapid territorial gains.
Yamamoto hoped Japan could then negotiate peace.
Japan launched coordinated attacks across the Pacific over a seven-hour period.
The coordinated attacks included the US-held Philippines, Guam, Wake Island, and Midway Atoll.
The coordinated attacks included British possessions in Malaya, Singapore, and Hong Kong.
Chūichi Nagumo commanded the attacking force.
The attack began at 7:48 a.m. Hawaiian time.
The article gives the attack's start time as 6:18 p.m. GMT.
A total of 353 Japanese aircraft struck the base.
The attacking aircraft included fighters, level bombers, dive bombers, and torpedo bombers.
The aircraft struck in two waves.
Six Japanese aircraft carriers launched the attacking aircraft.
Eight US battleships were present during the attack.
All eight US battleships present were damaged.
Four of the US battleships were sunk.
The article names USS Arizona and USS Utah as the ships that were not later refloated.
Six US battleships returned to service during the war.
The Japanese sank or damaged three cruisers.
The Japanese sank or damaged three destroyers.
The Japanese sank or damaged an anti-aircraft training ship.
The Japanese sank or damaged a minelayer.
More than 180 US aircraft were destroyed.
The attack killed 2,403 Americans.
The attack wounded 1,178 Americans.
Japan lost 29 aircraft.
Japan lost five midget submarines.
Japan lost 130 personnel.
All three US aircraft carriers assigned to Pearl Harbor were at sea during the attack.
The three absent US carriers were Enterprise, Lexington, and Saratoga.
Pearl Harbor's oil storage facilities were not attacked.
Pearl Harbor's naval repair facilities were not attacked.
Japan declared war on the United States later on the day of the attack.
Japan declared war on the British Empire later on the day of the attack.
It was already December 8 in Tokyo when Japan declared war.
Japan's declarations of war were not delivered until the day after the attack.
The United Kingdom declared war on Japan on December 8.
Germany declared war on the United States on December 11.
Italy declared war on the United States on December 11.
The Tripartite Pact with Japan did not formally obligate Germany or Italy to declare war on the United States.
The United States responded by declaring war on Germany.
The United States responded by declaring war on Italy.
Japan had previously taken military action without announcing it in advance.
The attack came without a formal warning.
The attack was perceived as unprovoked in the United States.
The lack of warning and the perception that the attack was unprovoked led President Franklin D. Roosevelt to call December 7, 1941, ‘a date which will live in infamy.’
Pearl Harbor remains Hawaii's deadliest disaster not caused by disease.
Pearl Harbor was the deadliest foreign attack on the United States for nearly 60 years, until the September 11 attacks in 2001.
War between Japan and the United States had been seen as possible since the 1920s.
Japan had been wary of US territorial and military expansion in the Pacific and Asia since the late 1890s.
The United States annexed Hawaii and the Philippines during its Pacific expansion.
Hawaii and the Philippines were close to or within what Japan regarded as its sphere of influence.
Japanese strategic thinkers believed economic self-sufficiency was necessary to wage modern war.
Japan drew from World War I the lesson that modern wars would be prolonged.
Japan drew from World War I the lesson that modern wars would require total mobilization.
Japan drew from World War I the lesson that modern wars would leave it vulnerable to trade embargoes.
Japan drew from World War I the lesson that modern wars would leave it vulnerable to encirclement.
Japan's home islands could not provide enough key resources such as iron and oil for its wartime needs.
Japan adopted a more hostile stance toward the United States after the rejection of the Racial Equality Proposal.
Japan and the United States continued to trade despite that hostility.
US–Japanese tensions did not rise sharply until Japan invaded Manchuria in 1931.
Japan expanded farther into China over the following decade.
Japan's expansion into China led to the Second Sino-Japanese War in 1937.
Japan devoted considerable effort to isolating China.
Japan sought independent access to enough resources to win the war on the Chinese mainland.
Japan designed the Southern Operation to help isolate China and secure resources.
Japan remained heavily dependent on oil imported from the United States.
US oil imports supplied Japanese forces in occupied Manchuria.
Stanley K. Hornbeck was chief of the US Division of Far Eastern Affairs.
Walter C. Teagle headed Standard Oil New Jersey.
Hornbeck reported on his meeting with Teagle to Roosevelt in a memorandum dated October 24, 1934.
Hornbeck described Teagle as uncooperative with US recommendations.
Hornbeck said the Japanese government gave Standard Oil special treatment.
Hornbeck said the special treatment made Standard Oil less subject to Japanese business regulations than other companies.
Hornbeck attributed the predominance of American petroleum in Japanese imports to Teagle's business dealings with Japan.
Western public opinion turned sharply against Japan starting in December 1937.
The Japanese attack on USS Panay helped turn Western opinion against Japan.
The Allison incident helped turn Western opinion against Japan.
The Rape of Nanjing helped turn Western opinion against Japan.
The United States unsuccessfully proposed a joint blockade of Japan with the United Kingdom.
American companies stopped providing Japan with implements of war in 1938 after an appeal by Roosevelt.
Japan invaded French Indochina in 1940 to obstruct the flow of supplies to China.
The United States halted shipments of airplanes to Japan in 1940.
The United States halted shipments of parts to Japan in 1940.
The United States halted shipments of machine tools to Japan in 1940.
The United States halted shipments of aviation gasoline to Japan in 1940.
Japan regarded the US shipment restrictions as unfriendly.
The United States initially continued exporting oil to Japan.
Washington partly held back from cutting off oil because it expected Japan's dependence on American oil to make such a cutoff seem extremely provocative.
Roosevelt moved the Pacific Fleet from San Diego to Hawaii in mid-1940.
Roosevelt ordered a military buildup in the Philippines.
Roosevelt hoped the fleet move and the buildup in the Philippines would deter Japanese aggression in the Far East.
Japan's high command mistakenly believed an attack on British colonies in Southeast Asia would automatically bring the United States into the war.
That belief led the Japanese high command to regard a preventive strike as the only way to stop US naval interference.
Japanese war planners considered an invasion of the Philippines necessary.
The American War Plan Orange envisioned defending the Philippines with 40,000 elite troops.
The proposed defense was not implemented because Douglas MacArthur opposed it.
MacArthur believed he would need ten times as many troops as the plan provided.
By 1941, American planners expected to abandon the Philippines at the outbreak of war.
Thomas C. Hart commanded the United States Asiatic Fleet.
Hart received orders late in 1941 to abandon the Philippines at the outbreak of war.
The United States stopped exporting oil to Japan in July 1941.
The US oil cutoff followed Japan's seizure of French Indochina after the fall of France.
New American restrictions on domestic oil consumption partly contributed to the oil cutoff.
The US oil cutoff prompted Japan to proceed with plans to seize the oil-rich Dutch East Indies.
On August 17, Roosevelt warned Japan that the United States was prepared to respond if neighboring countries were attacked.
The United States and Japan negotiated in 1941 in an effort to improve relations.
Japan offered to withdraw from most of China and Indochina after making peace with China's Nationalist government.
Japan proposed interpreting the Tripartite Pact independently.
Japan offered to refrain from trade discrimination if all other countries did the same.
Washington rejected those Japanese proposals.
Japanese Prime Minister Konoe offered to meet Roosevelt.
Roosevelt insisted on reaching an agreement before meeting Konoe.
The US ambassador to Japan repeatedly urged Roosevelt to accept Konoe's offer to meet.
The ambassador believed the meeting was the only way to preserve Konoe's conciliatory government.
The ambassador believed the meeting was the only way to preserve peace in the Pacific.
Roosevelt did not act on the ambassador's recommendation.
The Konoe government collapsed the following month.
The Konoe government collapsed when the Japanese military rejected a complete troop withdrawal from China.
Japan delivered its final proposal on November 20, 1941.
In its final proposal, Japan conditionally offered to withdraw from southern Indochina.
In its final proposal, Japan conditionally offered not to attack Southeast Asia.
The final proposal required the United States, United Kingdom, and Netherlands to supply Japan with one million US gallons, or about 3.8 million liters, of aviation fuel.
The final proposal required the United States, United Kingdom, and Netherlands to lift their sanctions against Japan.
The final proposal required the United States, United Kingdom, and Netherlands to stop aiding China.
The Hull note was the American counterproposal of November 26, which was November 27 in Japan.
The Hull note called for Japan's withdrawal from China to be complete and unconditional.
The Hull note called for Japan to conclude nonaggression agreements with Pacific powers.
Japan's planned military actions in Southeast Asia targeted overseas territories of the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and the United States.
Japan viewed the Pearl Harbor strike as a move it needed to make before its oil supplies ran out.
Preliminary planning for the Pearl Harbor attack began in early 1941 under Yamamoto.
The preliminary plan was meant to protect Japan's move into the Southern Resource Area.
Japan used ‘Southern Resource Area’ to refer to the Dutch East Indies and Southeast Asia generally.
Admiral Osami Nagano was chief of the Imperial Japanese Navy General Staff.
Yamamoto secured Nagano's assent to formal planning and training only after a dispute with Naval Headquarters.
Yamamoto threatened to resign his command during the dispute.
Full-scale planning was underway by early spring 1941.
Rear Admiral Ryūnosuke Kusaka did most of the full-scale planning.
Commander Minoru Genda helped plan the attack.
Captain Kameto Kuroshima helped plan the attack.
Kuroshima was Yamamoto's deputy chief of staff.
Japanese planners closely studied the 1940 British air attack on the Italian fleet at Taranto.
Japan trained pilots for the attack over the months that followed.
Japan adapted equipment for the attack over the months that followed.
Japan collected intelligence for the attack over the months that followed.
Emperor Hirohito first approved the attack plan on November 5, 1941.
Hirohito's initial approval followed the third of four Imperial Conferences held to consider the matter.
Hirohito initially hesitated to enter the war.
Hirohito approved the attack despite dissent from some advisers.
Hirohito gave final authorization for the attack on December 1, 1941.
Before final authorization, most Japanese leaders told Hirohito that the Hull note would undo Japan's gains in China.
Most Japanese leaders told Hirohito that the Hull note would endanger Manchukuo.
Most Japanese leaders told Hirohito that the Hull note would undermine Japanese control of Korea.
Hirohito became more involved in military affairs before the attack.
Hirohito took part in the Conference of Military Councillors, which was unusual for him.
Hirohito actively sought more information about war plans.
An aide said Hirohito openly showed happiness when told the surprise attacks had succeeded.
By late 1941, many observers thought war between the United States and Japan was imminent.
A Gallup poll just before the attack found that 52 percent of Americans expected war with Japan.
In the same poll, 27 percent of Americans did not expect war with Japan.
In the same poll, 21 percent of Americans had no opinion.
American Pacific bases and facilities had repeatedly been put on alert before the attack.
US officials doubted Pearl Harbor would be Japan's first target.
US officials expected Japan to attack the Philippines first.
US officials thought air bases in the Philippines threatened Japanese sea lanes and supply shipments from the south.
US officials thought the naval base at Manila threatened Japanese sea lanes and supply shipments from the south.
US officials mistakenly believed Japan could not mount more than one major naval operation at a time.
Japan intended to destroy major units of the US Pacific Fleet to keep it from opposing Japan's conquest of the Dutch East Indies and Malaya.
Imperial Japanese Navy leaders subscribed to Alfred Thayer Mahan's doctrine of decisive battle.
Japanese naval leaders wanted to destroy as many US battleships as possible.
Japan hoped the attack would buy time to consolidate its position.
Japan hoped the attack would buy time to build up its naval strength.
Japan believed US shipbuilding authorized by the 1940 Vinson-Walsh Act would eventually eliminate its chance of victory.
Japan targeted battleships in hopes of weakening America's ability to mobilize its forces in the Pacific.
Battleships were the prestige ships of navies at the time.
Japan hoped the attack would undermine American morale.
Japan hoped weakened American morale would lead Washington to drop demands that conflicted with Japanese interests.
Japan hoped weakened American morale would lead Washington to seek a negotiated peace.
Pearl Harbor's shallow water made it easier to salvage and potentially repair ships sunk at anchor.
Many sailors were expected to survive because they would be on shore leave or could be rescued from the harbor.
The absence of all three US carriers was an unexpected disadvantage for Japan.
Yamamoto decided to proceed despite the known disadvantages of attacking ships at anchor.
Pearl Harbor's navy yard was left undamaged.
Pearl Harbor's submarine base was left undamaged.
Japan spared some base facilities because it expected the war to end before those facilities could affect the outcome.
Kido Butai was the Japanese navy's Mobile Strike Force.
The Mobile Strike Force departed from Hittokapu Bay on Etorofu Island in the Kurils.
The article gives Iterup as the island's current name.
The six carriers were Akagi, Kaga, Sōryū, Hiryū, Shōkaku, and Zuikaku.
The Mobile Strike Force included two battleships.
The Mobile Strike Force included three cruisers.
The Mobile Strike Force included 11 destroyers.
The Mobile Strike Force included eight oilers.
Japan planned to attack Pearl Harbor with about 360 aircraft.
Japan planned for the first wave to be the main attack.
Japanese planners assigned fighters to defend the carrier force.
Japanese planners assigned aircraft to strike airfields as well as ships.
Two reconnaissance floatplanes came from the cruisers Chikuma and Tone.
Some historians consider the reconnaissance flights unnecessary.
Some historians argue that the reconnaissance flights risked alerting the Americans.
Japanese spy Takeo Yoshikawa had already reported on the composition of the US fleet at Pearl Harbor.
Yoshikawa had also reported on the fleet's readiness.
Tone's floatplane reported that the American fleet was not at Lahaina Roads.
The Japanese submarine I-72 also reported that the American fleet was not at Lahaina Roads.
Four additional Japanese floatplanes watched for a counterattack.
Five Japanese fleet submarines carried one Type A midget submarine each for the operation.
The five larger submarines were I-16, I-18, I-20, I-22, and I-24.
The five larger submarines left Kure Naval District on November 25, 1941.
The larger submarines reached waters near Pearl Harbor on December 6.
The midget submarines were launched early on December 7.
At 3:42 a.m. Hawaiian time, the minesweeper Condor spotted a midget submarine's periscope near the harbor entrance.
Condor alerted the destroyer Ward.
The midget submarine spotted by Condor may have entered Pearl Harbor.
Ward sank a different midget submarine at 6:37 a.m.
Ward fired the first American shots in the Pacific Theater.
A midget submarine near Ford Island fired a torpedo that missed the seaplane tender Curtiss.
The same submarine fired another torpedo that missed the destroyer Monaghan.
Monaghan sank the submarine at 8:43 a.m.
The midget submarine Ha-19 ran aground outside the harbor entrance.
Ha-19 ran aground a second time on the east side of Oahu.
Ha-19 was captured on December 8.
Japanese Ensign Kazuo Sakamaki swam ashore.
Hawaii National Guard Corporal David Akui captured Sakamaki.
Sakamaki became the first Japanese prisoner of war.
A depth charge attack damaged a fourth midget submarine.
The crew of the fourth midget submarine abandoned it before it fired any torpedoes.
The fourth midget submarine was found outside the harbor in 1960.
At 12:41 a.m. on December 8, Japanese forces received a radio message from a midget submarine.
The message claimed that the submarine had damaged one or more large warships inside Pearl Harbor.
Submersibles from the Hawaii Undersea Research Laboratory located sections of the fifth midget submarine in 1992, 2000, and 2001.
The fifth midget submarine's wreck lay in three pieces outside Pearl Harbor.
The wreck lay in a debris field where surplus American equipment had been dumped after the war.
The dumped equipment included vehicles and landing craft.
Both torpedoes were missing from the fifth midget submarine's wreck.
The article links the missing torpedoes to reports that two torpedoes were fired at the light cruiser St. Louis at 10:04 a.m. at the harbor entrance.
The article also links the missing torpedoes to a possible torpedo shot at the destroyer Helm at 8:21 a.m.

question.text: What was Japan trying to do by attacking Pearl Harbor?
quotes: Japan aimed to disable the US Pacific Fleet
was intended to disable the US Pacific Fleet
